summary: Describes the Coherent File Distribution Protocol (CFDP), an Experimental protocol for distributing files to many recipients.

eli5.summary: It is a way to hand out copies of the same file to many people at once.

questions: what is the coherent file distribution protocol
how does cfdp broadcast files to multiple clients
subtitle: Broadcast file distribution to reduce load when sending one file to many clients.

tldr.problem: Sending the same file to many clients one-to-one wastes server and network resources, and takes a long time. Examples include booting diskless workstations, distributing software updates, or sharing media in real-time conferences.
tldr.mechanism: CFDP runs on top of UDP and broadcasts file blocks to all interested clients at once. Clients listen for packets matching their ticket, checksum each block, and request any missing blocks from the server.
tldr.outcome: Multiple clients can receive a file in parallel over a single broadcast stream, reducing server load and transfer time compared to individual unicast transfers.

facts.label: Typical packet size
facts.value: 552 bytes (under IP MTU minimum of 576 bytes)

today: RFC 1235 is an Experimental protocol and has not been updated or obsoleted. It was designed for diskless workstations and local-area broadcast networks, and remains relevant for any scenario where identical files must be distributed to multiple recipients over a broadcast medium.

sections.title: The Problem of One-to-Many File Distribution
sections.content:
CFDP addresses a common networking challenge: efficiently distributing identical files to multiple recipients. When a server sends the same file to many clients using traditional one-to-one transfers, the server must open a separate connection and send the entire file n times, consuming server resources and network capacity proportionally to the number of clients.

The RFC describes practical scenarios where this becomes a bottleneck: diskless workstations booting simultaneously, software upgrades deployed to multiple machines at a site, or shared objects (documents, graphics, media) being sent to all participants in a real-time conference or classroom.

CFDP leverages broadcast networks (Ethernet, fiber, packet radio) to solve this problem, sending each block of data once over the broadcast medium where all interested clients can receive it together.
sections.eli5: Normally, to send a file to ten people, you send it ten separate times. CFDP is like announcing the file on a loudspeaker so everyone can listen in at the same time.

sections.title: How CFDP Works
sections.content:
CFDP is a protocol layer on top of UDP that manages file distribution over broadcast networks. When a client wants a file, it first contacts a ticket server (a separate protocol not strictly part of CFDP) to acquire a 32-bit ticket that uniquely identifies the file transfer, along with the block size (BLKSZ) and total file size (FILSZ). The ticket server also provides the addresses and UDP port numbers for the CFDP server and clients.

The client then listens on the client broadcast port for packets carrying its ticket. If no traffic appears within a timeout period (TOUT-1), it sends a full file request (FULREQ) to the server. The server responds by broadcasting the entire file in equal-sized blocks, each containing the ticket, block number, data length, a 32-bit checksum, and up to BLKSZ bytes of data. When the client receives a packet, it verifies the checksum, stores the block in the correct position in the file, and continues listening.

If the client detects missing blocks after a receive timeout (TOUT-2), it sends a partial file request (PARREQ) listing only the missing block numbers. The server then broadcasts just those blocks. This process repeats until all blocks arrive.
sections.eli5: A client asks for a ticket for the file it wants, then listens to the broadcast. The server shouts the file blocks one by one. If the client missed any, it asks the server to shout just those blocks again.

sections.title: Message Formats and Checksums
sections.content:
CFDP defines several message types. A FULREQ packet contains a 32-bit ticket, a 32-bit checksum, a function byte ('F'), a reserved byte, and a two-byte length field (zero for a full request). A PARREQ packet has the same header with function byte 'P' and contains a variable-length list of 16-bit block numbers to request. Data packets carry the ticket, checksum, 16-bit block number, 16-bit data length, and up to BLKSZ bytes of payload.

All numbers are in network byte order. The checksum is computed as the two's complement of the unsigned 32-bit sum (with no end-around-carry) of the rest of the packet. To verify, the receiver sums the entire packet including the checksum field, and the result should be zero. This simple checksum allows receivers to detect corruption without requiring a reliable transport protocol.

The RFC recommends BLKSZ of 512 or 1024 bytes. A 512-byte BLKSZ keeps the total packet size (IP header + UDP header + CFDP header + data = 20 + 8 + 12 + 512 = 552 bytes) well below the minimum IP MTU of 576 bytes, avoiding fragmentation. The 16-bit block number field limits files to 32 MB (with 512-byte blocks) or 64 MB (with 1024-byte blocks).
sections.eli5: Each packet has a label (ticket) so the client knows which file it is, a block number so the client knows where in the file it goes, and a check number so the client can tell if the data got scrambled.

sections.title: Client and Server State Machines
sections.content:
The client operates in four states: CLSTART (waiting for the first packet), RXING (receiving data), INCMPLT (incomplete; timed out during receive), and CLEND (transfer finished). From CLSTART, if no packet arrives within TOUT-1, the client sends a FULREQ and remains in CLSTART. When the first data packet arrives, the client moves to RXING. If no packets arrive during RXING within TOUT-2, it sends a PARREQ with missing block numbers and moves to INCMPLT. From INCMPLT, if another timeout occurs (TOUT-3), it retransmits the same PARREQ. When all blocks are received, the client enters CLEND and stops.

The server has two request-handling states: FULSND (sending the entire file in response to a FULREQ) and PARSND (sending only the blocks listed in a PARREQ). The server is otherwise in SIDLE (idle). When a FULREQ arrives, the server moves to FULSND and broadcasts all file blocks. When done, it returns to SIDLE. Similarly, PARREQ triggers PARSND. If multiple requests for the same file arrive during an active transfer, they are ignored; only one transfer of a given file proceeds at a time.
sections.eli5: The client waits, listens, and if nothing arrives in time, it yells for what it needs. The server either sends the whole file or just the missing pieces, then goes back to waiting.

sections.title: Packet Timing and Timeouts
sections.content:
CFDP performance depends on careful tuning of block size and timeout values. The RFC recommends keeping BLKSZ as a power of two for efficient offset computation, and smaller than the network MTU to avoid fragmentation. A good default is 512 bytes.

The server should insert a small delay between transmitted packets to avoid overwhelming clients' UDP buffers. The RFC suggests twice the transmission time of a single packet (estimated using ping) as a reasonable guideline.

Client timeouts are harder to predict. TOUT-1, TOUT-2, and TOUT-3 (the three timeout periods) should ideally be the same value. Experimental testing by the authors showed that 6 to 8 times the packet transmission time works well. Shorter timeouts risk mistaking transient network problems for loss, while longer timeouts delay the overall transfer. These parameters are implementation-dependent and may need adjustment for different network conditions and switch controllers.
sections.eli5: The server should not shout blocks too fast or the client will miss them. The client should wait long enough to be sure a block is really lost before asking again, but not so long that the whole transfer takes forever.

fields.name: Ticket
fields.desc: 32-bit identifier assigned by the ticket server.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: Two's complement checksum of the packet.

fields.name: Block Number
fields.desc: Offset in multiples of BLKSZ from the start of the file.

fields.name: Data Length
fields.desc: Octets in this packet; BLKSZ except for the last block.
